segments.label: §5 source sentence 1
segments.text: Ich fange daher mit der allgemeinen Darstellung des Baues der Amerikanischen Sprachen an, dergestalt, dass ich nach allen Richtungen hin, nach welchen Sprachen zu beurtheilen sind, die Eigenthümlichkeiten der Amerikanischen überhaupt, und die Verschiedenheiten der einzelnen unter sich vollständig anzugeben versuchen werde.

segments.label: §5 source sentence 2
segments.text: Auf diese Weise wird die Darstellung des Baues der einzelnen Sprachen in ihren hauptsächlichsten Theilen in die allgemeine verwebt, und nur das Unwesentlichere, und das, was die wahre Individualität der einzelnen Sprache ausmacht, die bestimmte Lautbezeichnung, fällt hinweg.

segments.label: §5 source sentence 3
segments.text: Auf der andren Seite wird allerdings bei diesem Verfahren die Schilderung der einzelnen Sprachen zerrissen, und eine vollständige Uebersicht des Baues einer jeden unmöglich gemacht.

segments.label: §5 source sentence 4
segments.text: Allein man gewinnt auch den Vortheil, jede Eigenthümlichkeit jeder einzelnen Sprache in dem allgemeinen Bilde gleich an der Stelle zu sehen, wo dieselbe mit denen der andren verglichen, und gewürdigt werden kann.

segments.label: §5 source sentence 5
segments.text: Wer gewohnt ist viele Sprachen in ihrem Bau zu erforschen, wird aber gerade diesen Vorzug kaum zu hoch anrechnen können.

segments.label: §5 source sentence 6
segments.text: Denn es ist eine der betrübendsten, aber darum nicht weniger gewöhnlichen Erfahrungen, wenn man sich mit Mühe und Anstrengung in den Bau einer Sprache hineingedacht hat, dennoch unschlüssig zu bleiben, wie man nun diese Sprache in dem Gebiete der ganzen Sprachkunde zu stellen, wie in der Verschiedenheit der gegen einander abzuwägenden Vorzüge und Mängel ihren Werth zu bestimmen hat.

segments.label: §5 source sentence 7
segments.text: Die Uebersicht, die wir so eben bei diesem Verfahren vermissten, lässt sich doch einigermassen durch ein zusammenstellendes Register wieder erlangen.

segments.label: §5 claude rendering 1
segments.text: I therefore begin with the general presentation of the structure of the American languages, in such a way that I shall attempt to state completely, along all the lines on which languages are to be judged, the peculiarities of the American languages in general and the differences of the individual languages among themselves.

segments.label: §5 claude rendering 2
segments.text: In this way the presentation of the structure of the individual languages is, in its principal parts, woven into the general presentation, and only the less essential, and that which constitutes the true individuality of the individual language, the determinate designation by sounds, falls away.

segments.label: §5 claude rendering 3
segments.text: On the other hand, this procedure does admittedly tear apart the portrayal of the individual languages and make a complete overview of the structure of each one impossible.

segments.label: §5 claude rendering 4
segments.text: Yet one also gains the advantage of seeing every peculiarity of every individual language, within the general picture, right at the place where it can be compared with those of the other languages and appraised.

segments.label: §5 claude rendering 5
segments.text: Anyone who is accustomed to investigating the structure of many languages will, however, hardly be able to rate precisely this advantage too highly.

segments.label: §5 claude rendering 6
segments.text: For it is one of the most distressing experiences, though no less common for that, that when one has with toil and exertion thought one's way into the structure of a language, one nevertheless remains undecided as to how one is now to place this language within the domain of the whole study of language, and how, amid the diversity of the merits and defects that are to be weighed against one another, one is to determine its worth.

segments.label: §5 claude rendering 7
segments.text: The overview that we just now found wanting in this procedure can nevertheless be regained to some degree by means of a collating index.

decision.question: Ambiguous referent. In 'into an understanding of a language's structure and yet remain uncertain how to place it ... how to determine its worth', the pronouns 'it' and 'its' can be read as the structure (or even the understanding). The German names the language as what is to be placed and valued.
decision.resolution: Name that language explicitly as the object to be placed; its worth then refers unambiguously to the language. Restore now and retain the modal is to be placed/determined.

decision.question: Merged terminological contrast. 'gewürdigt' is rendered 'assessed', the same word used for 'beurtheilen' in p5:s1. The German uses two different verbs, and 'würdigen' (to appraise, to give something its due value) anticipates 'ihren Werth zu bestimmen' in p5:s6. That link is lost and a false verbal echo with p5:s1 is created.
decision.resolution: Use appraised for gewürdigt, retaining its valuative connection with Werth. Assessed remains the local rendering of beurtheilen in sentence1; no universal one-to-one lexical rule is inferred.

decision.question: Potentially misleading English. Sentence-initial 'But', directly after 'Yet' in p5:s4, sets the sentence up as a counter to the advantage just named. Combined with 'scarcely ... value ... too highly', it invites the opposite reading, that such a person will hardly value it. The German reinforces the advantage: it can hardly be rated too highly. The 'aber' is a weak, clause-internal particle and 'gerade' is emphatic.
decision.resolution: Move however inside sentence5 and use rate this very advantage too highly. Preserve the scarcely qualification and the positive evaluation without an abrupt sentence-initial But.

decision.question: Weakened clause relation after the sentence split. 'dergestalt, dass' specifies the manner in which the general presentation is to be carried out ('in such a way that'). 'In doing so' presents the second statement as an accompanying action, so the specifying relation is no longer explicit.
decision.resolution: Restore a single sentence with in such a way that, explicitly making the attempted comprehensive account the manner of the general presentation.

decision.question: Referent of 'in its principal parts'. In English 'its' can be read as referring to 'the structure', which German grammar excludes. The German 'ihren' is itself ambiguous between 'Darstellung' (feminine singular) and 'der einzelnen Sprachen' (plural). The English silently picks the singular and leaves open a reading the source does not allow.
decision.resolution: Recast explicitly as the most important parts of the presentation. Note the alternative language antecedent; German ihren permits both Darstellung and Sprachen but excludes masculine Bau. Do not present the chosen antecedent as certain.

decision.question: Thinning of the allgemein/einzeln contrast (also affects p5:s3 and p5:s4). 'einzeln' is rendered 'individual' in p5:s1 and the first clause of p5:s2, but reduced to 'each language' for 'der einzelnen Sprache' (s2), 'der einzelnen Sprachen' (s3) and 'jeder einzelnen Sprache' (s4). The sense survives, but the paragraph's organising opposition between the general presentation and the individual languages is less visible. In p5:s3 the plural 'descriptions of the individual languages' also becomes distributive singular.
decision.resolution: Restore individual language(s) in sentences2–4 where it preserves the general/individual contrast at little cost.

decision.question: 'die bestimmte Lautbezeichnung' as 'its particular designation by sounds'. The possessive 'its' is added (the source has the definite article), and 'particular' for 'bestimmte' leans toward 'peculiar to it' where the German says 'determinate' or 'specific'. The apposition to 'what constitutes the true individuality' is correctly preserved. Whether 'Lautbezeichnung' means designation by means of sounds (most likely here) or the marking of sounds cannot be settled from this paragraph alone.
decision.resolution: Use the specific designation by sounds, removing the added possessive and retaining the apposition to true individuality. Record the designation-by-sounds reading as provisional, with sound notation as an unresolved alternative.

decision.question: Vortheil/Vorzug/Vorzüge. 'Vortheil' (s4) and 'Vorzug' (s5) are both 'advantage', while 'Vorzüge' (s6) is 'merits'. Because 'diesen Vorzug' in s5 refers back to the 'Vortheil' of s4, 'advantage' is defensible there and 'merits' suits 'Vorzüge und Mängel' as properties of languages. The German lexical link between s5 and s6 is not reproducible without cost. This is a judgment call, not an error.
decision.resolution: Retain advantage for the referring-back Vorzug in sentence5 and merits for Vorzüge in sentence6. Preserve the shared German root in this record and note the contextual choice rather than forcing one English noun.

decision.question: Small scope and term shifts. (a) 'the whole field of the study of language' attaches 'whole' to 'field', whereas 'ganzen' modifies 'Sprachkunde'. (b) 'study of language' (singular, abstract) for 'Sprachkunde' may suggest general theory of language where Humboldt's term is the knowledge or study of languages. (c) The asyndetic 'wie ..., wie ...' is joined with 'or'; 'and' would be more neutral. (d) 'unschlüssig' is nearer 'undecided' than 'uncertain'. None of these alters the claim.
decision.resolution: Use language study as a whole for the entire Sprachkunde, consistent with earlier study-of-language wording. Join the two questions with and and use remain undecided. Do not impose a modern disciplinary subfield.

decision.question: Explicitation. 'an index that brings the material together' supplies an object ('the material') for 'zusammenstellendes', which has none in the source. The addition is harmless, and the likely implied object is the scattered particulars of each language. 'Register' could also be a register or table, not strictly an index.
decision.resolution: Retain the descriptive index that brings the material together as a readable explicitation of zusammenstellendes. Note the supplied object and unresolved index/register format; preserve only partial recovery.

decision.question: Referent and degree are weakened: English 'in its principal parts' uses a singular pronoun readily taken with 'presentation' or 'structure', whereas German plural 'in ihren hauptsächlichsten Theilen' refers to the individual languages, and 'hauptsächlichsten' is superlative.
decision.resolution: Partly accept: make the referent explicit and restore most important for the superlative. Reject the assertion that German grammar requires plural languages: ihren fits feminine singular Darstellung or plural Sprachen. Choose presentation provisionally and record the alternative.

decision.question: Terminological contrast is collapsed: 'gewürdigt' is rendered 'assessed', the same word used for 'beurtheilen' in p5:s1, obscuring the distinction between assessing/judging languages in p5:s1 and appraising or duly valuing a characteristic here.
decision.resolution: Use appraised for the valuative gewürdigt while retaining assessed for beurtheilen in sentence1, on contextual grounds.

decision.question: The parallel German questions 'wie man ... zu stellen, wie ... ihren Werth zu bestimmen hat' present two connected objects of indecision. English 'how to place it ..., or how to determine its worth' can misleadingly suggest alternatives rather than two aspects of the same unresolved judgement.
decision.resolution: Join the two connected questions with and; the source supplies parallel wie clauses rather than an either-or choice.

decision.question: 'Uncertain' broadens 'unschlüssig', which denotes remaining undecided or unable to reach a conclusion, rather than general uncertainty or lack of knowledge.
decision.resolution: Use remain undecided about how to preserve the investigator’s inability to reach a conclusion rather than general lack of knowledge.

text_version.body: Ich fange daher mit der allgemeinen Darstellung des Baues der Amerikanischen Sprachen an, dergestalt, dass ich nach allen Richtungen hin, nach welchen Sprachen zu beurtheilen sind, die Eigenthümlichkeiten der Amerikanischen überhaupt, und die Verschiedenheiten der einzelnen unter sich vollständig anzugeben versuchen werde. Auf diese Weise wird die Darstellung des Baues der einzelnen Sprachen in ihren hauptsächlichsten Theilen in die allgemeine verwebt, und nur das Unwesentlichere, und das, was die wahre Individualität der einzelnen Sprache ausmacht, die bestimmte Lautbezeichnung, fällt hinweg. Auf der andren Seite wird allerdings bei diesem Verfahren die Schilderung der einzelnen Sprachen zerrissen, und eine vollständige Uebersicht des Baues einer jeden unmöglich gemacht. Allein man gewinnt auch den Vortheil, jede Eigenthümlichkeit jeder einzelnen Sprache in dem allgemeinen Bilde gleich an der Stelle zu sehen, wo dieselbe mit denen der andren verglichen, und gewürdigt werden kann. Wer gewohnt ist viele Sprachen in ihrem Bau zu erforschen, wird aber gerade diesen Vorzug kaum zu hoch anrechnen können. Denn es ist eine der betrübendsten, aber darum nicht weniger gewöhnlichen Erfahrungen, wenn man sich mit Mühe und Anstrengung in den Bau einer Sprache hineingedacht hat, dennoch unschlüssig zu bleiben, wie man nun diese Sprache in dem Gebiete der ganzen Sprachkunde zu stellen, wie in der Verschiedenheit der gegen einander abzuwägenden Vorzüge und Mängel ihren Werth zu bestimmen hat. Die Uebersicht, die wir so eben bei diesem Verfahren vermissten, lässt sich doch einigermassen durch ein zusammenstellendes Register wieder erlangen.

text_version.body: I therefore begin with the general presentation of the structure of the American languages, in such a way that I shall attempt to state completely, along all the lines on which languages are to be judged, the peculiarities of the American languages in general and the differences of the individual languages among themselves. In this way the presentation of the structure of the individual languages is, in its principal parts, woven into the general presentation, and only the less essential, and that which constitutes the true individuality of the individual language, the determinate designation by sounds, falls away. On the other hand, this procedure does admittedly tear apart the portrayal of the individual languages and make a complete overview of the structure of each one impossible. Yet one also gains the advantage of seeing every peculiarity of every individual language, within the general picture, right at the place where it can be compared with those of the other languages and appraised. Anyone who is accustomed to investigating the structure of many languages will, however, hardly be able to rate precisely this advantage too highly. For it is one of the most distressing experiences, though no less common for that, that when one has with toil and exertion thought one's way into the structure of a language, one nevertheless remains undecided as to how one is now to place this language within the domain of the whole study of language, and how, amid the diversity of the merits and defects that are to be weighed against one another, one is to determine its worth. The overview that we just now found wanting in this procedure can nevertheless be regained to some degree by means of a collating index.

In this way the presentation of the structure of the individual languages in its most principal parts is woven into the general presentation, and only what is less essential, and that which constitutes the true individuality of the individual language, the determinate designation of sounds, falls away. text_version.body: I therefore begin with a general account of the structure of the American languages, in which I shall attempt to give a complete account, in every respect in which languages are to be assessed, of the characteristics of the American languages generally and of the differences among the individual languages. In this way, the account of the structure of the individual languages is woven into the general account in its principal parts; only the less essential matters and that which constitutes the true individuality of each language—its particular expression in sounds—are omitted. On the other hand, this procedure does admittedly break up the description of the individual languages and make a complete overview of the structure of each impossible. Yet one also gains the advantage of seeing every characteristic of each individual language in the general picture at precisely the place where it can be compared with those of the others and assessed. Anyone accustomed to investigating the structure of many languages, however, will scarcely be able to value this particular advantage too highly. For it is one of the most disheartening experiences, though no less common for that, to have worked one's way, with effort and exertion, into an understanding of a language's structure, yet still remain uncertain how to situate that language within the whole field of linguistic knowledge, and how to determine its worth amid the diversity of merits and shortcomings that must be weighed against one another. The overview whose absence we have just noted in this procedure can nevertheless be recovered to some extent by means of an index that brings the material together.

In doing so, I shall try to set out fully, in every respect in which languages are to be assessed, the distinctive characteristics of the American languages as a whole and the differences among the individual languages. In this way, the presentation of the structure of the individual languages, in its principal parts, is woven into the general presentation; only the less essential matters and what constitutes the true individuality of each language—its particular designation by sounds—are left out. On the other hand, this procedure admittedly breaks up the description of each language and makes a complete overview of its structure impossible. Yet one also gains the advantage of seeing every distinctive characteristic of each language, within the general picture, at the very point where it can be compared with those of the other languages and assessed. But anyone accustomed to investigating the structure of many languages will scarcely be able to value this very advantage too highly. For it is one of the most disheartening experiences, though no less common for that, to have worked one’s way with effort and exertion into an understanding of a language’s structure and yet remain uncertain how to place it within the whole field of the study of language, or how to determine its worth amid the variety of merits and shortcomings to be weighed against one another. The overview we have just found lacking in this procedure can nevertheless be recovered to some extent through an index that brings the material together.
